sentences.text: Barilium was a robust iguanodontian dinosaur estimated to reach a length of 8 meters. Its genus name combines the Greek word for 'heavy' with the Latin term for 'ilium', reflecting its sturdy build.
The animal possessed large vertebrae featuring short neural spines, a structure that resembles those found in Camptosaurus.
Fossil remains of this species were discovered near St Leonards-on-Sea in East Sussex, England.
The specific name dawsoni honors Charles Dawson, the collector who found the holotype—the specimen the species is based on—in the 1880s.
Richard Lydekker first described Barilium as a species of Iguanodon in 1888.
David Norman later reclassified Barilium as a separate genus in 2010.
Barilium belongs to the unranked family Iguanodontia, with its parent group being the family Iguanodontidae.
Kenneth Carpenter and Yusuke Ishida independently assigned Barilium to the genus Torilion in 2010, making Torilion a junior synonym.
Phylogenetic analysis places Barilium outside the Hadrosauriformes clade, grouping it with Hypselospinus and Ouranosaurus.

Barilium lived approximately 138 million years ago during the Valanginian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Europe. Fossils come from the middle Valanginian-age Lower Cretaceous Wadhurst Clay.
The time range for Barilium spans from the Valanginian to the Barremian, between 137.05 and 121.4 million years ago.
